hello.title: Hello, Prolog
hello.summary: Write your first Prolog program and print text with writeln, write and format.
hello.lesson.0: Prolog is a **logic programming** language. Instead of telling the computer step by step what to do, you describe facts and rules, and then you ask questions. First, you learn how a Prolog program prints text.
hello.lesson.2: The first line is a **directive**: a line that starts with `:-` runs while Prolog loads the file. `initialization(main, main)` means: when the file is loaded, run `main` and then stop. Every program in this course starts with this line.
hello.lesson.3: `main :- writeln('Hello, Prolog!').` defines `main`. Read `:-` as "is true if": `main` is true if Prolog can print the text. Every **clause** ends with a full stop `.`, like a sentence. `writeln` prints a value and then a new line.
hello.lesson.5: Text in single quotes, like `'Hello, Prolog!'`, is an **atom**: a constant name. A word that starts with a lowercase letter, like `hello`, is an atom too, even without quotes. Text in double quotes, like `"A string"`, is a **string**. For printing, both work the same.
hello.lesson.7: A comma `,` between goals means **and then**: Prolog runs the goals from top to bottom. `write` prints a value without a new line, and `nl` prints only a new line.
hello.lesson.9: `format` prints a format text. Inside it, `~w` is replaced by the next value from the list in square brackets `[ ]`, and `~n` starts a new line. When there is no `~w`, you can leave out the list.
hello.lesson.11: Inside a rule, separate the goals with commas. Only the last goal ends with a full stop. A full stop too early ends the clause, and the next line becomes a new, broken clause. Also, `format` never adds a new line by itself: end the text with `~n`.
hello.lesson.12: In the exercises, the directive `:- initialization(main, main).` is often left out to keep the code short. Imagine it at the top of the file.
hello.card.1: `main :- Goal1, Goal2.` the comma means and then
hello.card.2: `writeln(X)` prints with a new line, `write(X)` without, `nl` = new line
hello.card.4: Every clause ends with a full stop `.`
hello-1.explain: `write` prints without a new line, so `a` and `b` appear next to each other. `nl` ends the line.
hello-2.explain: Each `~w` is replaced by the next value from the list: first `1`, then `2`.
hello-3.statement: Every clause in Prolog ends with a full stop `.`.
hello-3.explain: A clause is like a sentence: it ends with a full stop. Without it, Prolog reports a syntax error.
hello-4.prompt: Complete the program so it runs `main` and prints `Ready`.
hello-4.explain: The directive `:- initialization(main, main).` runs `main` when the file is loaded and then stops.
hello-5.explain: The two `~w` are replaced by `ab` and `cd` with nothing between them, so the result is `abcd`.
hello-6.prompt: The program should print `one` and `two`. Which line has the bug?
hello-6.explain: The full stop after `writeln(one)` ends the clause too early. Use a comma: `writeln(one),`.
hello-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hello, world`.
hello-7.explain: The head `main :-` comes first. The goals run from top to bottom, and the last goal ends with a full stop.
hello-8.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-8.pairs.0: prints X and a new line
hello-8.pairs.1: prints X without a new line
hello-8.pairs.3: the next value in a format text
hello-8.pairs.4: a new line in a format text
hello-9.prompt: Build the goal that prints `Hi bo`.
hello-9.explain: `format` takes the format text and then the list of values. `~w` becomes `bo`, and `~n` ends the line.
hello-10.prompt: In `main :- write(a), write(b).`, what does the comma mean?
hello-10.options.0: and then: run the next goal
hello-10.options.1: or: run one of the goals
hello-10.options.3: a new line in the output
hello-10.explain: A comma between goals means and then. Prolog runs `write(a)` first and then `write(b)`.
hello-11.explain: The single quotes make one atom, `'Big Cat'`. `writeln` prints it without the quotes.
hello-12.statement: `format` adds a new line at the end of the output by itself.
hello-12.explain: `format` prints exactly what you write. Add `~n` at the end of the format text for a new line.
facts.title: Facts and queries
facts.summary: Describe a small world with facts and ask Prolog questions about it, with and without variables.
facts.lesson.0: A **fact** says that something is true. The fact `likes(ann, pizza).` says: Ann likes pizza. `likes` is the name of a **predicate**, and `ann` and `pizza` are its **arguments**, separated by commas. Names start with a lowercase letter, and every fact ends with a full stop.
facts.lesson.2: These four facts are a small **database**. Loading them prints nothing: facts only describe the world. To learn something, you ask a **query**. In the interactive Prolog shell, you type a query after the prompt `?-`. `?- likes(ann, pizza).` answers `true`, and `?- likes(bob, soup).` answers `false`, because no fact says so.
facts.lesson.3: In a program, you write a query as a goal. When the goal succeeds, the next goal runs. When it fails, the rest of `main` does not run.
facts.lesson.6: A **variable** starts with an uppercase letter or `_`, for example `X` or `Food`. In a query, a variable asks: which value makes this true? `?- likes(ann, X).` answers `X = pizza`. Prolog looks through the facts from top to bottom and stops at the first one that matches. In the shell, you type `;` to get the next answer: `X = salad`.
facts.lesson.8: To get **all** answers in a program, use `forall(Query, Action)`: it runs `Action` once for every answer of `Query`. You learn more about it in the last unit.
facts.lesson.10: The **anonymous variable** `_` means: any value, I do not care which. `likes(Who, _)` asks who likes anything. Ann appears twice because two facts match.
facts.lesson.12: Prolog names a predicate by its name and its number of arguments: `likes/2` means `likes` with two arguments. `likes/2` and `likes/3` are different predicates.
facts-1.prompt: Which answer does `?- color(grass, C).` give?
facts-1.explain: Only the fact `color(grass, green).` matches, so `C` becomes `green`.
facts-2.statement: With these facts, the query `?- animal(cow).` answers `true`.
facts-2.explain: Prolog only knows what the facts say. No fact says `animal(cow)`, so the answer is `false`.
facts-3.explain: The only fact with `salad` is `likes(ann, salad).`, so `X` becomes `ann`.
facts-4.prompt: Which of these is a variable?
facts-4.explain: Variables start with an uppercase letter or `_`. `food` and `'Food'` are atoms, and `"Food"` is a string.
facts-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints every animal.
facts-5.explain: The query and the action must use the same variable `A`. Then `writeln(A)` prints the value of each answer.
facts-6.explain: A predicate name must start with a lowercase letter. Write `parent(bob, ann).`.
facts-7.prompt: How many answers does `?- parent(tom, X).` give?
facts-7.explain: Two facts start with `parent(tom, ...)`: `X = bob` and `X = liz`.
facts-8.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
facts-9.prompt: The `likes` facts are loaded. Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ann likes pizza`.
facts-9.explain: The query must run first, so that `Food` has a value when `format` prints it.
facts-10.prompt: Build the fact that says: Bob likes soup.
facts-10.explain: A fact is the predicate name, the arguments in parentheses and a full stop. `bob` must be lowercase, or it would be a variable.
facts-11.statement: With the facts `likes(ann, pizza).` and then `likes(ann, salad).`, the first answer to `?- likes(ann, X).` is `X = pizza`.
facts-11.explain: Prolog tries the facts from top to bottom, so the first matching fact gives the first answer.
facts-12.explain: Two facts match `likes(_, pizza)`, so `write(x)` runs twice.
rules.title: Rules
rules.summary: Write rules that derive new knowledge from facts, combine goals with and, or and not, and choose with if-then-else.
rules.lesson.0: A **rule** says that something is true if other things are true. It has a **head** and a **body**: `Head :- Body.` Read `:-` as "if". The goals in the body are joined with commas, which mean **and**.
rules.lesson.2: Read the rule like this: `X` is a grandparent of `Z` if `X` is a parent of some `Y` and `Y` is a parent of `Z`. Inside one clause, the same variable name always means the same value. In another clause, `X` is a new, unrelated variable.
rules.lesson.4: A predicate can have several clauses. Prolog tries them from top to bottom, and each one can make the predicate true. So several clauses mean **or**: here, something is a pet if it is a cat or if it is a dog.
rules.lesson.6: Inside a body, `;` also means **or**, but separate clauses are usually easier to read. `\+` means **not**: `\+ Goal` succeeds when `Goal` fails.
rules.lesson.9: `( Condition -> Then ; Else )` runs `Then` when `Condition` succeeds, and `Else` when it fails. The arrow `->` means **then**. Put the whole construction in parentheses.
rules.lesson.11: A variable that appears only once in a clause is called a **singleton**. It is often a typo, so SWI-Prolog prints a warning. When you really do not need the value, write `_` or start the name with `_`.
rules.lesson.12: Keep all clauses of one predicate together in the file. When other clauses come between them, SWI-Prolog prints a warning.
rules.card.2: Several clauses = several ways to be true
rules.card.4: Same name in one clause = same value
rules-1.prompt: How do you read `:-` in `happy(X) :- sunny, rested(X).`?
rules-1.explain: `happy(X)` is true if the body is true. `:-` means if, and the comma in the body means and.
rules-2.explain: Tom is a parent of Bob, and Bob is a parent of Ann, so Tom is a grandparent of Ann.
rules-3.statement: With these two clauses, `pet(rex)` is true if `rex` is a cat or if `rex` is a dog.
rules-3.explain: Prolog tries both clauses. If one of them succeeds, `pet(rex)` is true. Several clauses mean or.
rules-4.prompt: Complete the rule: a bird flies if it is not a penguin.
rules-4.explain: `\+ Goal` succeeds when `Goal` fails. So `\+ penguin(X)` means: `X` is not a penguin.
rules-5.explain: The goals in a body must be separated by commas. Write `parent(F, C),`.
rules-6.prompt: Which answer does `?- pet(X).` give first?
rules-6.explain: Prolog tries the clauses from top to bottom. The first clause asks `dog(X)`, and the first dog fact is `dog(rex).`.
rules-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so `check(tweety)` prints `yes` and `check(rex)` prints `no`.
rules-7.explain: The condition comes first, then `->` with the then part, then `;` with the else part, and the closing parenthesis ends the clause.
rules-8.prompt: Match the symbol with its meaning.
rules-9.prompt: Build the rule: `X` is a pet if `X` is a cat.
rules-9.explain: The head `pet(X)` comes first, then `:-` (if), then the body `cat(X)` and a full stop.
rules-10.explain: Pingu is a bird, but `penguin(pingu)` is true, so `\+ penguin(pingu)` fails. `flies(pingu)` fails, and the else part prints `no`.
rules-11.statement: Inside one clause, every `X` stands for the same value.
rules-11.explain: A variable name refers to one value in the whole clause. In another clause, the same name is a new variable.
rules-12.prompt: Why does SWI-Prolog print a warning for `pet(X) :- cat(Y).`?
rules-12.options.0: `X` and `Y` each appear only once in the clause
rules-12.options.1: A rule needs at least two goals
rules-12.options.2: `pet` must first be defined as a fact
rules-12.explain: A variable that appears only once is a singleton and is often a typo. Here it should be `pet(X) :- cat(X).`.
unification.title: Unification
unification.summary: Understand how = matches values and structures, gives variables their values, and when matching fails.
unification.lesson.0: In Prolog, `=` does not assign a value. It **unifies**: it tries to make both sides equal by giving variables values. `X = hello` succeeds and `X` gets the value `hello`. `5 = 5` succeeds, and `5 = 6` fails.
unification.lesson.2: Once a variable has a value, it keeps it for the rest of the clause. `X = 1, X = 2` fails, because `1` cannot be made equal to `2`. Unification works in both directions: `5 = X` is the same as `X = 5`.
unification.lesson.4: A **compound term** is a name with arguments, like `point(3, 4)` or `date(2024, 5, 17)`. It looks like a fact, but here it is data. Two structures unify when they have the same name, the same number of arguments, and each pair of arguments unifies.
unification.lesson.6: Unification fails when the names differ or when the number of arguments differs. `point(1, 2) = pair(1, 2)` fails, and so does `point(1, 2) = point(1, 2, 3)`. Variables may appear on both sides: `point(X, 2) = point(1, Y)` gives `X = 1` and `Y = 2`.
unification.lesson.8: Queries use unification too. When Prolog looks for a matching fact, it unifies the query with each fact. So you can put structures into facts and pick out parts of them.
unification.lesson.10: `==` checks whether two terms are already **identical**, without giving any variable a value. `\=` succeeds when two terms cannot be unified, and `\==` when they are not identical.
unification.lesson.12: `X = 1 + 2` does not calculate. It unifies `X` with the structure `1 + 2`, so `writeln(X)` prints `1+2`. You learn how to calculate in the next unit.
unification.card.2: Different name or number of arguments: fails
unification-1.explain: The structures have the same name and two arguments each, so `A = 7` and `B = 8`. The code prints `B` first.
unification-2.explain: `=` only unifies. `X` becomes the structure `2 + 3`, which prints as `2+3`.
unification-3.explain: `point(1, 2)` has two arguments and `point(1, 2, 3)` has three, so they cannot be unified.
unification-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `1`.
unification-4.explain: `=` unifies the two structures, so `X` becomes `1`. `==` and `\=` do not give variables values, and `is` calculates.
unification-5.explain: `X = Y` links the two variables. When `Y` becomes `cat`, `X` is `cat` too.
unification-6.prompt: The program should print `3 4` and then `3`. Which line has the bug?
unification-6.explain: `point(Z)` has one argument, but `point(3, 4)` has two, so the unification fails. Write `point(Z, _) = Point`.
unification-7.prompt: What are `X` and `Y` after `f(X, b) = f(a, Y)`?
unification-7.explain: The arguments are unified pair by pair: `X` with `a`, and `b` with `Y`.
unification-8.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
unification-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `1` and then `2`.
unification-9.explain: The unification must come first, so that `X` and `Y` have values when they are printed.
unification-10.prompt: Build the query that finds the title `T` of the book from 1965.
unification-10.explain: The query has the same shape as the facts: `book(title(T), year(1965))`. Unification fills in `T`.
unification-11.explain: Structures unify only when the names are the same. `point` and `pair` are different names.
unification-12.explain: `==` does not give `X` a value. At first `X` has no value, so it is not identical to `5`. After `X = 5`, it is.
arithmetic.title: Arithmetic
arithmetic.summary: Calculate with is, compare numbers, and use arithmetic inside rules to find prices and totals.
arithmetic.lesson.0: To calculate, use `is`. `X is 2 + 3` first calculates the right side and then unifies `X` with the result, `5`. You can use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and parentheses. `//` divides whole numbers without the rest, and `mod` gives the rest.
arithmetic.lesson.2: `*` comes before `+`, as in mathematics. `7 / 2` gives the decimal number `3.5`. The right side of `is` must be fully known: `X is Y + 1` gives an error when `Y` has no value yet.
arithmetic.lesson.3: A variable cannot change its value, so `X is X + 1` never works. Use a new variable for each new value, for example `Total` and then `NewTotal`.
arithmetic.lesson.6: To compare numbers, use `=:=` (equal), `=\=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `>=` and `=<` (less or equal; careful, not `<=`). These operators calculate both sides first. So `1 + 2 =:= 3` succeeds, but `1 + 2 = 3` fails, because the structure `1+2` is not the number `3`. The helper `check` below uses `call(Goal)`, which runs a term as a goal.
arithmetic.lesson.9: Rules can calculate and compare. The result of a calculation is an extra argument of the predicate: `cost(Item, Count, Cost)` finds the price and calculates `Cost`.
arithmetic.lesson.11: There are also functions: `max(3, 7)`, `min(3, 7)`, `abs(-4)` and `sqrt(16)`. `sqrt` always gives a decimal number, and a calculation with a decimal number gives a decimal number.
arithmetic.lesson.13: `=` never calculates. `is` calculates only its right side and unifies the result with the left side. To compare two calculations, use `=:=`.
arithmetic-2.explain: `mod` gives the rest of the division: 17 = 3 * 5 + 2.
arithmetic-3.explain: `/` gives a decimal number when the division is not exact. Use `//` for a whole-number result.
arithmetic-4.explain: `=` does not calculate: the structure `2+2` is not the number `4`. `2 + 2 =:= 4` succeeds.
arithmetic-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `yes`.
arithmetic-5.explain: `=<` means less than or equal, so `3 =< 3` succeeds. Prolog has no `<=` operator.
arithmetic-6.prompt: The program should print `Next: 6`. Which line has the bug?
arithmetic-6.explain: `=` does not calculate, so `Next` would be `5+1`. Write `Next is Count + 1,`.
arithmetic-7.prompt: Which goal sets `X` to the result of 3 times 4?
arithmetic-7.explain: `is` calculates the right side and puts the result into the variable on the left.
arithmetic-8.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
arithmetic-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `9`.
arithmetic-9.explain: `W` needs a value before `is` can calculate `W * W`, and `A` needs a value before it is printed.
arithmetic-10.prompt: Build the goal that sets `Rest` to 10 minus 4.
arithmetic-11.explain: A melon costs `5`, so `Cost is 5 * 3` gives `15`.
arithmetic-12.statement: `X is Y + 1` works even when `Y` has no value yet.
arithmetic-12.explain: `is` needs every value on the right side. Without a value for `Y`, Prolog reports an error.
recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Repeat work with recursive rules: count down, calculate factorials and sums, and find ancestors.
recursion.lesson.0: Prolog has no loops. To repeat something, a rule calls itself: this is **recursion**. A recursive predicate needs a **base case**, which stops the recursion, and a **recursive case**, which solves a smaller problem.
recursion.lesson.2: `countdown(0)` is the base case: it prints `go`. For any other number, the second clause prints `N`, calculates `N1`, one less, and calls `countdown(N1)`. The **guard** `N > 0` makes sure that the second clause does not apply to `0` or to negative numbers.
recursion.lesson.4: The factorial of a number is the product of all numbers from 1 to it: `5!` is `5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1`. The rule is: `0!` is `1`, and `N!` is `N` times `(N-1)!`. Because predicates do not return values, the result is an extra argument `F`.
recursion.lesson.6: For `factorial(3, F)`, Prolog needs `factorial(2, F1)`, which needs `factorial(1, ...)`, which needs `factorial(0, ...)`. The base case gives `1`, and then each waiting clause multiplies: `1 * 1`, `2 * 1`, `3 * 2` = `6`. The same pattern adds up all numbers from 1 to `N`:
recursion.lesson.9: Recursion also works on facts. An ancestor is a parent, or a parent of an ancestor. The first clause is the base case, and the second clause takes one step up the family tree and then calls `ancestor` again.
recursion.lesson.11: Every recursive call must make progress towards the base case. A rule like `ancestor(X, Y) :- ancestor(Z, Y), parent(X, Z).` calls itself before anything else and never stops. Put a goal that makes progress, like `parent(X, Z)` or `N1 is N - 1`, before the recursive call.
recursion.lesson.12: Prolog integers have no size limit, so `factorial(30, F)` gives the exact result.
recursion.card.1: Recursive case: smaller problem, then call itself
recursion.card.3: Result in an extra argument: `factorial(N, F)`
recursion-2.prompt: Which part of the factorial program is the base case?
recursion-2.explain: The base case is the clause that does not call `factorial` again: the factorial of `0` is `1`.
recursion-3.explain: There is no base case, and `count` always calls itself again. The recursion never stops.
recursion-4.explain: `is` calculates `N * F1` and gives `F` the result. `=` would build the structure `5*(4*...)` instead of a number.
recursion-5.prompt: `sum_to(N, S)` should add up the numbers from 1 to `N`. Which line has the bug?
recursion-5.explain: The sum of no numbers is `0`, not `1`. Write `sum_to(0, 0).`, otherwise every result is one too big.
recursion-6.prompt: How many answers does `?- ancestor(b, X).` give?
recursion-6.explain: `b` is a parent of `c`, and `c` is a parent of `d`. So the answers are `X = c` and `X = d`.
recursion-7.prompt: The factorial predicate is loaded. Put the lines in order so the program prints `120`.
recursion-7.explain: `N` needs its value `5` before `factorial` can use it, and `F` needs its value before it is printed.
recursion-8.prompt: Match the part of the factorial program with its role.
recursion-9.prompt: Build the goal that sets `N1` to one less than `N`.
recursion-9.explain: `N1 is N - 1` calculates the smaller number for the next recursive call.
recursion-10.prompt: Why does this rule never stop?
recursion-10.options.0: It calls itself first, before a goal that makes progress
recursion-10.explain: `ancestor(Z, Y)` calls the same rule again with nothing changed, again and again. Put `parent(X, Z)` first and add a base case.
recursion-12.statement: `factorial(30, F)` gives the exact result, a number with 33 digits.
recursion-12.explain: Prolog integers have no size limit, so the result `265252859812191058636308480000000` is exact.
lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Store values in lists, split them into head and tail, use member, append and length, and write list recursion.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds values in square brackets, separated by commas: `[apple, banana, cherry]`. `[]` is the empty list. The pattern `[H|T]` splits a list into its first element, the **head** `H`, and the list of the remaining elements, the **tail** `T`.
lists.lesson.2: `writeln` prints lists without spaces. The tail is always a list: for `[cherry]`, the head is `cherry` and the tail is `[]`. The empty list `[]` has no head, so it never matches `[H|T]`. `[X, Y|Rest]` takes the first two elements at once.
lists.lesson.4: SWI-Prolog has many list predicates. `length(L, N)` counts the elements, `member(X, L)` succeeds when `X` is an element of `L`, `append(A, B, C)` joins `A` and `B` into `C`, and `reverse(L, R)` reverses a list.
lists.lesson.6: These predicates also work with variables. `member(X, L)` gives every element of `L` as an answer. `append(A, B, [1, 2])` finds every way to split `[1, 2]` into two parts.
lists.lesson.9: Most list predicates follow one pattern: a base case for the empty list `[]` and a recursive case for `[H|T]` that handles the head and calls itself on the tail. `count` counts the elements, and `total` adds them up.
lists.lesson.11: A predicate can also build a new list. `double` takes `[H|T]` and builds `[D|DT]`, where `D` is the doubled head and `DT` is the doubled tail.
lists.lesson.13: You cannot define your own predicate with the name of a built-in one like `length/2`: SWI-Prolog reports a permission error. Choose another name, like `count`.
lists.card.1: `[]` is the empty list and never matches `[H|T]`
lists-1.explain: The head is `a` (here ignored with `_`), and the tail `T` is the list of the remaining elements, `[b,c]`.
lists-3.explain: `append` joins the elements of both lists into one flat list.
lists-4.statement: The empty list `[]` matches the pattern `[H|T]`.
lists-4.explain: `[H|T]` needs at least one element for `H`. The empty list has none.
lists-5.prompt: Complete the base case so `total([4, 5, 6], S)` gives `S = 15`.
lists-5.explain: The recursion ends with the empty list, and the sum of no numbers is `0`.
lists-6.explain: The recursive call must work on the tail `T`, not on the head `H`. Write `double(T, DT).`.
lists-7.explain: `b` is an element of `[a, b, c]`. `[a]` is a list, not the element `a`, and the empty list has no elements.
lists-8.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists-8.pairs.2: N is the number of elements
lists-8.pairs.3: C is A followed by B
lists-8.pairs.4: X is an element of L
lists-9.prompt: The base case `show([]) :- nl.` is given. Put the lines in order so `show([a, b, c])` prints `<a><b><c>`.
lists-9.explain: For each element, the clause prints `<`, the head and `>`, and then handles the tail with the recursive call.
lists-10.prompt: Build the pattern that splits a list into its head `H` and its tail `T`.
lists-10.explain: `[H|T]` puts the first element into `H` and the remaining list into `T`.
lists-11.prompt: How many lines does this print?
lists-11.explain: `[x, y]` can be split in three ways, so `A` is `[]`, `[x]` and `[x,y]`.
lists-12.explain: `double` doubles every element: `5` becomes `10` and `10` becomes `20`.
collecting.title: Collecting solutions
collecting.summary: Use backtracking to get every answer, and collect answers with findall, forall and between.
collecting.lesson.0: When a goal fails, Prolog goes back to the last place where it had a choice and tries the next possibility. This is called **backtracking**. The goal `fail` always fails, so it forces Prolog to try every answer.
collecting.lesson.2: `member` gives `1`, `writeln` prints it, and `fail` sends Prolog back to `member` for the next element. When there are no more elements, the left side of `;` fails, and the right side `true`, which always succeeds, lets the program continue.
collecting.lesson.3: `between(Low, High, X)` gives every integer from `Low` to `High`, one after another. With `forall`, the action can be several goals in parentheses.
collecting.lesson.6: `findall(Template, Goal, List)` finds every answer of `Goal` and collects `Template` for each answer in `List`. When there is no answer, `List` is `[]`. The template can be a structure, like the pair `N-A`, and several goals go in parentheses.
collecting.lesson.8: With the list predicates from the previous unit, you can calculate with all answers: count them with `length` or add them up with `sum_list`.
collecting.lesson.11: `forall(Condition, Action)` succeeds when `Action` succeeds for every answer of `Condition`. So it can also check a property of all answers, for example that everyone is older than 10.
collecting.lesson.13: The variables inside `findall` and `forall` get no values outside of them. Only the result list of `findall` keeps the collected values.
collecting.card.0: `findall(X, Goal, L)` collects every answer in `L`
collecting.card.1: `forall(Cond, Action)` runs or checks for every answer
collecting-1.explain: For every `X` in the list, `findall` collects `Y`, which is `X * 10`.
collecting-2.explain: `between(2, 5, X)` gives `2`, `3`, `4` and `5`, so the list has four elements.
collecting-3.explain: `findall` always succeeds. When the goal has no answers, the list is empty.
collecting-4.explain: `between` gives every integer from the low to the high value, both included.
collecting-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[2,4,6]`.
collecting-5.explain: `=:=` calculates `X mod 2` and compares it with `0`, so only the even numbers stay.
collecting-6.prompt: The `age` facts for three people are loaded. The program should print `3`. Which line has the bug?
collecting-6.explain: `findall` needs a third argument for the result list. Write `findall(Name, age(Name, _), Names),`.
collecting-7.prompt: Which goal collects all names from the `age` facts into `Names`?
collecting-7.explain: The first argument of `findall` is what you collect, the second is the goal, and the third is the result list.

collecting-8.pairs.1: A for every answer of C
collecting-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `start`, then `1`, `2`, `3`, then `done`.
collecting-9.explain: The goals run from top to bottom: first `start`, then the numbers from `forall`, then `done`.
collecting-10.prompt: Build the goal that collects the numbers from 1 to 5 in `L`.
collecting-10.explain: `findall` collects `X` for every answer of `between(1, 5, X)` into `L`.
collecting-11.explain: `fail` makes Prolog backtrack into `member` for every element, so `write` prints `a`, `b` and `c` on one line.
collecting-12.explain: Every element of `[2, 4, 6]` is even, so the check succeeds for every answer of `member`.
